jobs.text: Those fucking rent-seeking hyperscalers took the internet away from you, and we’re going to give it back to you and to everyone. Web 1.0 was great - we had IRC, file sharing, third party chat clients. There were personal websites, forums. Flash was a format kids could use. Everything supported embedding and uploading. Websites actually had APIs and RSS. File sharing, FTP, MP3s, discs, owned media. Broadband brought our parents and grandparents online, but the shift to the non-technical majority created an opportunity to grossly oversimplify everything. Everything dumbed down into a pre-packaged product. Startups began turning their offerings into walled gardens. Platforms took precedence over protocols. APIs and access and data export went away. And then the rent-seeking began. The era of ownership ended. Corporate Memphis. Jesus Christ. We’ve rallied a massive community to build MIT/Apache-licensed alternatives to Adobe, Microsoft Office, Google Workspace, Autodesk, SolidWorks, Slack, Discord, Unreal Engine, OpenRouter, RunPod, and more. The goal is full feature parity, with code anyone can own, inspect, modify, and build on. We’re digesting second-class apps and platforms into first-class applications, libraries, and APIs with full MCP support. We’re distilling out the good parts, and we’re building the connective tissue that draws them together. 100% of the internet is going to be open source soon, and we’re going to force it open. Loudly. We have eight figures in run rate revenue, over 20M app downloads and growing. Our community is the best part, and it’s energetic like a wildfire. Everyone resonates with our mission. We’re missionaries, not mercenaries. We are going to slay the incumbents by being better. Our motto is Google’s old motto - “Don't be evil (tm)”. We’re a tiny team looking for strong engineers to own major parts of the product: desktop apps, lots of completely open source backend infrastructure, agent workflows, agentic app factories. Stack: Rust, a sprinkle of TypeScript/React, egui, Tauri, MySQL/Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, Kubernetes. Lots and lots of Rust. We’re systems engineers by trade, but we like to vibe code Rust. Did I say Rust? Rust. Rust Rust Rust. Maybe that's a filter. You have to be self-directed and independent. If you want to open source Salesforce with half your time, do it! If you want to work on Solidworks 3D printing applications, great! Writing music apps and DAWs? Go for it! Custom Discord/Slack clients for our custom, completely open source chat API and platform? Hell yeah. Our organization is flat, and we're going to go after everybody and everything. Everything you build here will be open source. We have no private repos. We can reclaim the internet. That’s our mission. Want to know more about us? Look up “Adobe ArtCraft” on YouTube / TikTok / your platform of choice. If this resonates with you, email hn@storyteller.ai with your Github, a little about yourself and something you’ve built. Write the sentence, “don’t take my RAM, Sam!” so we know you’re one of the good guys.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Spark RPC TLS (spark.ssl.rpc.enabled) loads entire disk-cached blocks into memory, causing executor OOMs
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: We're moving our Spark 4.1.1 jobs from our current setup, which uses AES-based RPC encryption ( spark.network.crypto.enabled=true ), to RPC TLS ( spark.ssl.rpc.enabled=true ). With RPC TLS, jobs that cache data with persist( StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY ) and then read it from other executors started getting executors OOMKilled. The same jobs run fine with our current AES setup. From the code, it looks like this is the cause. When an executor sends a disk-cached block to another executor, DiskBlockData ( DiskStore.scala ) does this ( link to DiskStore.scala ): override def toNetty(): AnyRef = new DefaultFileRegion(file, 0, size) // without TLS: streams the file override def toNettyForSsl(): AnyRef = toChunkedByteBuffer(ByteBuffer.allocate).toNettyForSsl // with TLS: reads the whole block into memory So with TLS, sending a 1.5 GB block first copies all 1.5 GB onto the heap, and the read also needs a temporary direct buffer of the same size. A few of those at once is enough to push an executor over its container limit. To confirm it, I ran the same test job twice, once with AES and once with TLS. It caches 24 partitions of 1.5 GB, then has executors fetch each other’s partitions. Each executor had 8 GB of heap and a 10 GB container: AES TLS Executor OOM kills 0 5 Peak memory per executor 1.9 GB 10 GB (the limit) Peak heap 1.6 GB 8 GB (full) Peak direct memory ~0 4.5 GB Allocation profiles from the TLS run show where the memory came from: DiskBlockData.toNettyForSsl → ByteBuffer.allocate accounted for about 40% of all heap allocations, and JavaUtils.readFully → FileChannelImpl.read accounted for about 90% of all direct memory allocations. Neither shows up in the AES run. Every OOM kill happened right as executors started fetching blocks from each other. What I've already tried: Setting -Djdk.nio.maxCachedBufferSize=262144 stops the JDK from caching the temporary direct buffers after each read. It helped a lot in our real jobs: OOM kills went from hundreds per run to a handfu
